title: Maryland religious leaders call for continuing conversations after Michigan synagogue attack
summary: After last week's shooting at a Michigan synagogue, Maryland faith leaders were called upon to discuss the situation, and what can be done. But they say it's a conversation that needs to be had all the time, not just after the latest crisis.
content:
by Rhiannon Evans, Maryland Matters March 15, 2026

by Rhiannon Evans, Maryland Matters March 15, 2026

Ron Halber, CEO of the Jewish Community Relations Council of Greater Washington, was on the phone all morning Friday talking to reporters about the attack on a synagogue in West Bloomfield, Michigan, the day before.

He understands it’s part of the job, and he does it willingly. He just wishes the conversation continued, even after the outrage of the moment has passed and the cameras have moved on.

“There’s got to be a much more vibrant civic communication taking place among leaders, and it has to be ongoing,” Halber said. “It can’t just be that an incident happens, the media focuses attention on it, we talk about it, and it goes away, and then we wait for the next incident.”

Zainab Chaudry, director of the Maryland chapter of the Council on American-Islamic Relations, agreed.

“We as a state and we as a community have to come together and have the hard conversations on what is driving anger,” Chaudry said. “And the hatred and the pain that is fueling hate within our society.”

Their comments came after a driver struck the side of Temple Israel, before opening fire on the synagogue in Michigan on Thursday. The security team at the temple shot and killed the suspected shooter. One security guard was shot during the attack, but none of the children or staff who were inside the synagogue during the attack were hurt.

“We are deeply and humbly grateful to our teachers, staff, security, law enforcement and Shenandoah Country Club that welcomed us, fed us and sheltered our staff, teachers, children and parents,” Temple Israel said in a statement on its Facebook page after the attack.

YOU MAKE OUR WORK POSSIBLE.

Maryland Gov. Wes Moore lamented the attack in a Facebook post. He said hate has no place in our communities, and urged people to speak out against antisemitism whenever they see it happening.

“At a time when Jewish communities across our country are faced with rising antisemitism, an attack on a house of worship is an attack on the very heart of our nation,” Moore said in the post.

Hate crimes against Jews have risen sharply in Maryland in recent years, jumping from 77 in in 2022 to 284 in 2023 and 276 in 2024, according to Maryland State Police data. That report said anti-Jewish hate crimes accounted for 28.5% of all hate crimes in 2024, trailing only attacks against Blacks.

Religious institutions and other potential targets of hate crimes have had to harden their security in response.The state Protecting Against Hate Crimes program, for security at houses of worship and nonprofit facilities, was doubled from $5 million last year to $10 million this year, and Moore included the higher figure in his fiscal 2027 budget plan.

When hateful rhetoric builds, it polarizes communities and serves as a breeding ground of opportunity for acts of violence to be committed against vulnerable communities, according to Halber.

“When language is used to attack any ethnic minority or faith groups, it should be roundly condemned by people across the spectrum,” Halber said. “Elected officials from both parties should be tripping over each other to get to a microphone to condemn it.”

Chaudry echoed that sentiment and said that communities need to come together and have hard conversations about what’s driving the hate and anger fueling these attacks.

“Whether that’s hate directed towards Muslim communities, whether it’s directed towards Palestinians, whether it’s directed towards Arab Americans, whether it’s directed towards Jewish Americans – our communities have so much more in common than we have what sets us apart,” Chaudry said.

She also noted that legislation like Sen. Shelly Hettleman’s (D–Baltimore County) Senate Bill 308 would help start those conversations. The bill would require an annual proclamation by the governor, designating January as Muslim American Heritage month and May as Jewish American Heritage month.

Hettleman said her bill and any similar bills, in addition to breaking down barriers among cultural groups, would “shine a light on the contributions of cultural communities, such as our Muslim and Jewish communities.”

“Anytime we can highlight diversity, that is a good thing,” Hettleman said.

Halber said that the violence in Israel has led to increasing attacks against Jewish communities, who are trying to cope.

“You learn to live with it,” he said. “Nobody is happy about it, but it doesn’t prevent us from going about and living our lives, proudly, as Jews.”
